newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Low-income women put fashion foot forward at work.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Low-income women put fashion foot forward at work.

text.p: For former prison inmate Charline Brundidge, getting together the right clothes for her first job interview was as intimidating as her new freedom.

But with the help of a programme that puts haute couture on the average Jane, Brundidge and scores of other low-income women are putting their best fashion foot forward, shedding their ordinary clothes for Chanel and other top designers.

"Finding an outfit was not in the uppermost part of my mind when I was getting ready to leave prison," Brundidge, now an administrative assistant at a programme for battered women, said at the recent kick-off for Dress For Success New York.
"But when I came across a job opportunity I realised how hard it would be to buy something to wear that would make me feel like I belonged."
In December, the 49-year-old Brundidge became the first woman in New York history to be granted clemency after being convicted of killing the husband who battered her.
NICE CLOTHES MEAN FEELING GOOD
"Having nice clothes helped me feel good about myself," said Brundidge, who had spent 10 years of a 15-year-to-life sentence in prison and was Dress For Success' first client.

Based in a cramped basement apartment in New York's popular Greenwich Village district, the programme provides each low-income woman with one designer suit for job interviews and a second one when she gets a job.

The organisation, which works by referral from other non-profit agencies, allows women a chance to browse through racks of new and used clothes that include $1,000 suits from Chanel, Ann Taylor and Eileen Fisher. On the floor by the door are shoes donated by designer Kenneth Cole.
"Dignity should not be something that only rich women have. It is something everyone should be able to accrue," Nancy Lublin, an energetic founder of the group, said.
"We only take clothes that are new or that have been cleaned and pressed. First impressions really matter and this has harsh consequences for low-income women," added Lublin, a full-time law student.
INSPIRED BY 'POPPY MAX'

She said the idea to start the programme was inspired by her great-grandfather, "Poppy Max," who immigrated to the United States from Eastern Europe just before the First World War and spent his first two weeks sleeping under the Brooklyn Bridge.

During the Depression, "Poppy Max" peddled household items out of a cart, creating an ad-hoc lay-away system of payment. "When he died, I wanted to capture his faith in people and his understanding of personal struggle," Lublin said.

The 25-year-old woman captured that spirit in Dress For Success, which since its start a few months ago has outfitted more than 300 women who have suffered from violence, poverty and loss. The group has also helped women find jobs in a range of workplaces from banks to hospitals.
"It's a little like being Cinderella -- only they don't have the glass slippers," said Jo-Anne Jones, also a former prison inmate recently helped by Dress For Success.
For many non-profit groups, Dress For Success is a good example of a private group providing support for people who need it at a time of cutbacks in government welfare programmes.

"This is a time of maximum emergency," said activist and writer Gloria Steinem, an advisory board member of Dress For Success. "The is about the power of the personal. To help make women feel like they are unique individuals."
For Lublin as well, to look good means to feel good.
"To me," she said, "it's more about feeling good. To see women stand before the mirror and see their shoulders go back three inches and then watch them strut out the door."
